title: British railway mania, 1840s
subtitle: Original lines and lines authorised 1844-45
description: The original-lines result depends heavily on asset life and terminal value, which are judgement inputs. See the verdict fragility panel.
asOfRule: Last quarter-end before the primary railway share index peak (6 October 1845, per Campbell). Uses hindsight. To be applied the same way to later cases.
hindsightDisclosure: Scored by someone who knew the outcome: that railway shares peaked in 1845 and fell by about two-thirds by 1849, and that the new lines cost more and earned less than promised.

sources.citation: The Railway Chronicle, 16 August 1845, p. 1015, table of railway lines authorised in 1845.
sources.note: Known to the case author only through Odlyzko (2012, note 7); original not opened.

sources.citation: Odlyzko, A. (2012). The Railway Mania: Fraud, disappointed expectations, and the modern economy, revised 14 Aug 2012, Table 1, derived from Tooke and Newmarch, A History of Prices, vol. 5 (1857), p. 352.
sources.note: Only the 1844 row is used: 2,240 miles in service, £35,700 construction cost per mile, £3,280 revenue per mile; later rows are not used.

sources.citation: Odlyzko, A. (2011). The collapse of the Railway Mania, the development of capital markets, and the forgotten role of Robert Lucas Nash, Accounting History Review 21(3), pp. 309-345 (SSRN 1625738), Hyde Clarke revenue per mile series.
sources.note: Only the 1842-1844 values are used: £3,036, £3,081, £3,283. Publication date approximate.

sources.citation: Odlyzko, A. (2010). Collective Hallucinations and Inefficient Markets: The British Railway Mania of the 1840s (SSRN 1537338).
sources.note: Used for: long-term government bond yield of about 3% at the end of 1844; authorised mileage of 805 in 1844 and about 2,700 in 1845 (the 1845 figure differs across sources, 2,700 to 2,896; verify against the paper). Publication date approximate. Series end 1845-08-31 to verify: that the 1845 session closed in August 1845.

York and North Midland shareholders' committee: lines authorised before 1845 earned 7.65% after interest on debt, those authorised in 1845 earned 4.15%, those authorised in 1846 earned 0.07%. Publication date approximate.

Share index fell from 167.9 in summer 1845 to 60.5 at the end of 1849, a drop of 64% (Gayer, Rostow and Schwartz, 1953, as reported); East Anglian lines planned at £8,786 and £1,070 revenue per mile, actual £18,342 per mile and £687 revenue per mile in 1855; revenue on new lines largely £1,000-1,500 per mile; actual costs 50% to 100% above promoters' estimates.

sources.citation: Managerial failure in early Victorian Britain: Network and capital expansion during the Railway Mania, Business History (2022), doi 10.1080/00076791.2022.2096877.
sources.note: Author names to be added when verified. Publication date approximate, latest possible. Reports that all of the York and North Midland's 1844-45 authorisations were unremunerative.

pool.note: (2,240 miles x £3,280 + 3,500 miles x £1,670) / 1,000 = £13.19m a year; new lines at the promoters' £1,670 a mile.

speed.note: Authorised lines expected to be built over several years; no source found for the legal completion deadlines; high sensitivity.

mid.note: Same rationale as adoption speed: authorised lines expected to be built over several years; no source found for the legal completion deadlines.

disc.note: Long-term government bonds yielded about 3% at the end of 1844 (C3); 2 points added for equity risk; no source for the premium.

premium.note: No share price is sourced for 30 September 1845; 0 tests the economics at replacement cost, not whether the market price was too high.

tvGrowth.note: Long-lived infrastructure; implied multiple 20x at a 5% rate; growth of 0 is a placeholder.

evidence.note: Revenue per mile rose from £3,036 (1842) to £3,081 (1843) and £3,283 (1844).

offset.note: Chosen so the modelled year-0 revenue (about £7.08m) is close to the 1844 actual of £7.35m.

capex.note: 2,240 miles x £35,700 per mile = £79.97m, the replacement cost of the network at 1844 construction costs.

outcomes.summary: For: assets earned decent returns: the York and North Midland committee found its pre-1845 lines earned 7.65% after interest (O1). Against: shareholders at the peak lost: the railway share index fell 64% between summer 1845 and the end of 1849 (O2).

The committee found 4.15% for lines authorised in 1845 and 0.07% for those authorised in 1846 (O1); new lines' revenue was largely £1,000-1,500 per mile and costs ran 50-100% above plan (O2); all of the company's 1844-45 authorisations were unremunerative (O3).
